newsitem.title: INDIA: Simplified clearance seen for Indian air cargo.
newsitem.headline: Simplified clearance seen for Indian air cargo.

text.p: The Indian Commerce Ministry has released final details of a study recommending to the national Planning Commission simplified government clearance for Private Air Cargo (PAC) operators setting up their own units.
This follows the directorate-general of civil aviation announcing at end-February that it would allow private Indian domestic carriers to operate foreign cargo routes.

Commerce Ministry officials said the recommendations would provide one-stop clearance instead of going through the present 22 different agencies - the most difficult being land acquisition, land use, nomination of the custodian by Customs, clearance of customs staff, data connections,and quarantine arrangements.

The study recommends a clear divide between airline and custodian roles, with prior declaration of theft-prone cargo by shippers. Proposed facilities would include closed circuit tv and special security areas.
Setting up a comprehensive data collection system would help forecasts and planning for individual products, it adds.

It also said improved road access at airports is necessary together with new, long-term air cargo investment by the public sector. And in the meantime it calls for the expansion of both the public and private sectors of the industry, with temporary facilities where necessary.

Industry sources said there is a clear need for upgrading cargo facilities in many areas of the country but when the Commerce Ministry's first draft recommendations emerged in mid-1996, there was little response from the private sector.
Further, some industry sources have suggested that improvements in export cargo management since January 1996 at existing terminals mean private investors would need to balance cost against return.

An Airport Authority of India (AAI) source said that if the proposals to streamline government clearances for the PAC were taken on board, then investment in private units would clearly reduce the AAI's own investment needs.
But the AAI is already understood to be planning to build on its success since January last year in dramatically increasing the speed of export cargo throughput, he added.

However, the result could be that by 1998 private investors find the return on investment too low. But a return could be made by investing in building bonded warehousing away from airports in collaboration with Customs, the industry sources added.
